title: Customer Support AI Agent
summary: Helping support operators move from an EV charging issue to a grounded diagnosis and a guided next step.
problem: Support teams need to combine live charger information with troubleshooting knowledge. A useful assistant must select the right tools, ground its answers in returned data, and ask focused questions when an issue is unclear.
contribution: As part of the chargeMOD team, I contributed to the support platform described in my résumé: hybrid retrieval, live API validation, fuzzy charger-name resolution, and streamed responses across multiple reasoning paths.

decisions.title: More than one path to an answer
decisions.body: The documented pipeline selects between direct diagnosis from logs, retrieval of troubleshooting procedures, and guided questioning. The response path follows the evidence available for the issue.

decisions.title: Combine keyword and semantic retrieval
decisions.body: BM25 and ChromaDB provide complementary retrieval signals, followed by cross-encoder reranking to select relevant troubleshooting material.

decisions.title: Ground operational details
decisions.body: Live tool responses validate identifiers and account details before they enter the answer context. The architecture separates model reasoning from the systems that execute actions.

outcome: My résumé reports approximately 50% lower average support resolution time for the team-built platform.
evidence_note: Reported résumé outcome; the measurement period and evaluation dataset are not included in the supplied material. The diagram is a conceptual explanation, not an internal deployment map.

title: Conversational Analytics Agent
summary: Turning questions about charging operations into scoped analytics through predefined tools.
problem: Charging operators need answers about energy, sessions, and faults without repeatedly navigating dashboards. Natural-language access must still respect the user's authorized data scope.
contribution: I contributed to the team's conversational analytics agent, including parameterized query functions, caching, pre-aggregation, reliability controls, and prompt-regression evaluation described in my résumé.

decisions.title: Predefined queries
decisions.body: The assistant selects from prepared, parameterized tools instead of generating arbitrary SQL. This keeps data access bounded and makes each query behavior testable.

decisions.title: Access scope belongs to the application
decisions.body: The application supplies authorized context to analytics tools. The model does not decide which customer's data it may access.

decisions.title: Responsiveness and evaluation
decisions.body: Redis caching and nightly pre-aggregation reduce repeated work. The résumé describes a 95% prompt-regression accuracy requirement as a deployment gate, not a universal accuracy claim.

outcome: The résumé describes the agent serving 1,700+ daily active users through 15–20 parameterized query functions.
evidence_note: Usage and tool-count figures are reported in the supplied résumé. Local architecture documents describe evolving access-scoping implementations; this case study presents only the shared principle.

title: DataPilot AI
summary: Turning a question about a CSV into SQL, a readable explanation, and a chart—with a route back when a query fails.
problem: Exploring a new dataset often means switching between a spreadsheet, a SQL editor, and a charting tool. I wanted to explore how one question-led interface could connect those steps while making the generated query visible.
contribution: I built a Streamlit application around a LangGraph workflow, with separate modules for SQL generation, execution, explanations, follow-up questions, and visualization. The repository includes tests for the database, agents, graph, and chart helpers.
architecture: Upload a CSV and inspect its schema
Execute the query; route errors back for a bounded retry
Choose a chart and suggest follow-up questions

decisions.title: Recovery is part of the graph
decisions.body: Generation and execution have separate routing functions. Query errors can return to generation with error context, instead of treating every failed attempt as the end of the interaction.

decisions.title: Keep the data layer separate
decisions.body: A database module owns schema inspection and query execution. The documented read-only restrictions are part of the prototype design, rather than an authorization decision delegated to the language model.

decisions.title: Choose charts from the result shape
decisions.body: A dedicated visualization module selects and creates bar, line, pie, and scatter charts. This keeps presentation logic inspectable alongside the query and explanation.

outcome: A public application prototype connecting dataset upload, conversational querying, error recovery, and visual explanation.
evidence_note: Reviewed against the public README and graph, database, agent, and visualization modules. The application and its tests were not executed during this portfolio review; README benchmark claims are not reproduced.

title: Enterprise Guild
summary: Coordinating project requests, budget checks, and human approval through a structured agent workflow.
problem: A useful planning assistant needs more than a plausible assignment. It needs to consult available resources, represent its decision in a structured format, and stop when a person must approve the next step.
contribution: I explored this through an ADK agent pipeline with MCP tools for department budgets and team capacity, a structured QuestCard output, and a custom GuildJuryAgent for approval. The public repository also includes evaluation and integration-test scaffolding.
architecture: Pause for approval when the workflow requires it

decisions.title: Ground plans in tools
decisions.body: Budget and capacity queries are exposed through a FastMCP server backed by SQLite. The prototype uses a local mock resource database.

decisions.title: Represent the approval pause explicitly
decisions.body: The agent implementation uses request-input and resumability primitives so that a human decision can become part of the workflow.

decisions.title: Give the result a schema
decisions.body: A Pydantic QuestCard describes the output structure. An additional review stage explores checking the generated assignment before returning it.

outcome: A public orchestration prototype showing tool-grounded planning and a human approval boundary.
evidence_note: Based on the public README, agent implementation, and MCP tool definitions. This is a personal prototype with mock data; production use, security guarantees, and evaluation results have not been established here.

title: Sales & Feasibility AI Agent
summary: Connecting site analysis, financial calculations, and proposal creation for EV infrastructure.
problem: Evaluating an EV charging site combines location context, market information, installation costs, operating costs, and financial projections. These inputs then need to become a coherent proposal.
contribution: My résumé describes contributions to a sequential Site, Market, Financial, and Proposal Writer agent workflow, with Python tools handling geolocation, market metrics, and financial calculations.

decisions.title: Calculate outside the language model
decisions.body: Financial calculations belong to deterministic tools. The language model coordinates the workflow and explains results instead of inventing financial values.

decisions.title: Make the output reviewable
decisions.body: Proposal creation turns analytical results into a document that a person can review. Current reference documentation also describes an editable presentation workflow.

decisions.title: Keep project versions distinct
decisions.body: The résumé describes a CrewAI-based workflow and PDF proposals. Newer documentation describes an evolved proposal studio with Word and PowerPoint output; those are project-level developments rather than additional individual ownership claims.

outcome: A team-built workflow that brings feasibility analysis and proposal preparation into one process.
evidence_note: No independently measured conversion or time-saving metric was supplied. Descriptions distinguish the résumé version from the newer documented system.

title: Voice Support Architecture
summary: A voice-oriented support design that separates conversational orchestration from reliable operational tools.
problem: A caller experiences latency differently from someone reading a chat window. Voice support needs short spoken responses, safe operational actions, and a clear way to handle slower work.
contribution: I contributed as an AI engineer to this team project. This overview explains the documented architecture; the supplied résumé does not identify individual ownership of specific voice modules.

decisions.title: Separate conversation from execution
decisions.body: A voice orchestrator manages the conversation while a layered tool service handles operational requests. Tool boundaries make responsibilities explicit.

decisions.title: Render critical facts into speech
decisions.body: Templates turn tool results into spoken responses for operational facts. Longer requests can return a pending state with a short spoken acknowledgement.

decisions.title: Explicit states for consequential actions
decisions.body: The server owns the confirmation sequence for actions. The conversational model follows that state instead of deciding whether required steps can be skipped.

outcome: The architecture is designed around a roughly 1.5-second voice-turn response budget.
evidence_note: This is a documented design target, not a verified latency result or a claim of production deployment. The walkthrough uses a fictional scenario.

title: Dynamic Tariff & Demand Forecasting
summary: Connecting network demand forecasts to bounded pricing decisions at individual chargers.
problem: Demand varies across locations and time. A pricing system needs to account for network trends and individual charger behavior while keeping adjustments within defined limits.
contribution: I contributed to the nightly forecasting and pricing pipeline described in my résumé, including model selection, charger profiling, preprocessing, and bounded tariff adjustments.

decisions.title: Model at two levels
decisions.body: Network-wide forecasts compare XGBoost, Random Forest, and Prophet. Per-charger decisions combine activity classification with log-space energy regression.

decisions.title: Represent different charging patterns
decisions.body: KMeans clusters 36-feature charger profiles. Outlier clipping and log transformation help handle skewed demand data.

decisions.title: Constrain the final decision
decisions.body: The résumé describes asymmetric sigmoid adjustments bounded between −6% and +12%. A model output becomes a pricing input within explicit limits.

outcome: The résumé reports approximately 10% revenue uplift alongside peak-hour load suppression.
evidence_note: Reported résumé outcome; the supplied material does not include a measurement window or controlled attribution analysis.

title: Cloud Data Pipeline & Analytics
summary: A partitioned analytics pipeline connecting charging transactions to daily business reporting.
problem: Growing transaction volumes make repeated analytics queries expensive. A reporting pipeline also needs to handle late-arriving records, reruns, and unexpected data shapes.
contribution: I contributed to the nightly ETL pipeline described in my résumé, including partitioned transformations, repeatable writes, late-data handling, and dashboard refreshes.

decisions.title: Match storage to queries
decisions.body: Date-partitioned Parquet reduces the amount of data scanned by analytical queries. AWS Glue and PySpark handle the nightly transformation.

decisions.title: Design for reruns and late data
decisions.body: Idempotent partition overwrites make repeated processing predictable. A 48-hour lookback buffer incorporates recent late-arriving transactions.

decisions.title: Separate anomalous records
decisions.body: Schema-anomaly quarantine keeps unexpected records visible for follow-up while supporting the regular reporting process.

outcome: The résumé reports approximately 95% lower cloud query costs and 30% less ETL processing time, with 1M+ transactions processed nightly.
evidence_note: Reported résumé outcomes; baseline workloads and billing evidence are not part of the supplied material.

title: Operational & Retention Analytics
summary: Making charger uptime and customer lifecycle changes visible to operational teams.
problem: Operations teams need to spot gaps in charger availability, while customer teams need to recognize changes in charging activity and organize follow-up.
contribution: My résumé describes work on uptime batch processing, schema handling, churn detection, lifecycle clustering, calling-console support, and retention reporting as part of the team.

decisions.title: Compute availability from activity gaps
decisions.body: Daily jobs account for AC/DC schema differences and configurable gap thresholds, with idempotent batch updates.

decisions.title: Track changes across customer lifecycles
decisions.body: Monthly energy-drop thresholds and rolling-percentile clustering organize users into five activity tiers.

decisions.title: Connect analytics to follow-up
decisions.body: A calling console, call-outcome records, and Power BI views support operational decisions and customer recovery work.

outcome: The résumé reports approximately 20% lower operational downtime in connection with the uptime-monitoring work.
evidence_note: Reported résumé outcome. The supplied material does not establish a measured churn-reduction percentage.

title: ControlGym
summary: Exploring reinforcement learning and classical control on a mass–spring–damper system.
problem: How do learned controllers compare with classical control when the system model changes or measurements become noisy? A simple physical system provides a repeatable setting for that question.
contribution: This personal repository brings together controller implementations, benchmark scripts, system identification, and an interactive dashboard.

decisions.title: Compare multiple approaches
decisions.body: The repository documents PPO, SAC, and TD3 alongside PID, LQR, and MPC, with a hybrid RL/PD approach.

decisions.title: Explore robustness
decisions.body: Documented experiments include parameter variation, sensor noise, and impulse disturbances. These expose behavior beyond a single idealized setup.

outcome: A public environment for exploring controller behavior, benchmarking, and system identification.
evidence_note: This summary is based on the public repository documentation. It does not claim that one controller universally outperforms another.

title: Diabetic Retinopathy Classification
summary: Comparing deep-learning models for retinal fundus image classification.
problem: Retinal images provide a practical setting for studying representation learning and multi-class image classification.
contribution: This personal project explores multiple deep-learning architectures in published notebooks for classifying retinal fundus images.

decisions.title: Compare model families
decisions.body: The public project describes EfficientNet, VGG16, DenseNet, ResNet50, and MobileNetV2 experiments.

decisions.title: Define the classification task
decisions.body: The repository describes three categories: No DR, Mild DR, and Severe DR. The portfolio follows that public description rather than conflicting older summaries.

outcome: Public notebooks documenting a medical-image classification learning project.
evidence_note: A research and learning project; no clinical deployment or diagnostic performance is claimed here. Older portfolio accuracy figures are omitted because their evaluation context has not been verified.

title: WellTrack AI
summary: Connecting wellness assessments, historical trends, and downloadable reports in one application prototype.
problem: A standalone model notebook does not show how someone enters information, revisits earlier records, or makes use of a result. This project explores those surrounding application workflows in a wellness-tracking context.
contribution: I built assessment and history views with Streamlit, relational persistence with SQLAlchemy, Plotly charts, and PDF/CSV report exports. Separate modules explore model training, prediction, and assessment notifications.

decisions.title: Make history part of the experience
decisions.body: The interface retrieves previous assessments and risk records so that the application can show changes over time, rather than only a single prediction.

decisions.title: Separate the app from the training experiments
decisions.body: The main interface uses rule-based scoring. The separate training module compares classifiers and ensemble approaches; its presence does not imply that every trained model is connected to the app.

decisions.title: Provide a useful artifact
decisions.body: PDF and CSV exports make assessment records portable. Reporting and notification logic live in their own modules.

outcome: A public wellness-application prototype that connects forms, persistence, charts, and reports with separate machine-learning experiments.
evidence_note: Reviewed from the README and application, training, prediction, and notification code structure. No clinical validation or real-world health outcome is claimed; model performance has not been independently reproduced.

title: Pneumonia Image Classification
summary: Exploring how different pretrained vision backbones approach chest X-ray classification.
problem: An image-classification experiment involves more than choosing a network. Input preparation, augmentation, class balance, and training controls all influence how useful the comparison will be.
contribution: I developed local Jupyter and Google Colab notebooks that explore pretrained networks including VGG16, DenseNet121, MobileNetV2, InceptionV3, and InceptionResNetV2 for chest X-ray classification.
architecture: Prepare and split the image dataset
Train with callbacks and class weighting
Review model behavior within the notebook

decisions.title: Compare several representations
decisions.body: The notebooks use multiple pretrained convolutional architectures. This makes backbone choice an experimental variable rather than a fixed assumption.

decisions.title: Treat training controls as part of the experiment
decisions.body: ImageDataGenerator, class-weight utilities, early stopping, and learning-rate callbacks appear in the implementation, alongside the classification layers.

decisions.title: Keep the experiment inspectable
decisions.body: The public repository includes both local and Colab notebook versions, so the preparation and training steps can be examined directly.

outcome: A public transfer-learning study connecting image preparation, backbone comparison, and controlled training.
evidence_note: Verified against the two public notebooks and repository description. This is an educational image-classification project; no clinical deployment, diagnostic reliability, or independently reproduced accuracy is claimed.
